properties.description:
- **`matchBook_eq`**: `Router.matchBook ext key m env w` does exactly one thing. It calls `ext.call_IPoolManager_unlock ext.POOLMANAGER (matchBookData key m)` and throws away the result. `matchBookData` is the encoded callback: action 4 (MatchBook), the five pool key fields, then seven zero words for the placeholder order, then `maxMatches`.
- **`matchBook_revert_iff`**: it reverts only when the `unlock` call reverts, and with the same error.
- **`matchBook_ok_iff`**: it succeeds with final state `w'` exactly when `unlock` succeeds and ends in `w'`. The Router adds no state change of its own.
properties.title: Router.matchBook

properties.description:
- **`fillFromPoolLiquidity_eq`**: the function only does two things. First it writes two transient (per-transaction) slots: `USER_LOCATION` gets the caller and `ASYNC_FILLER_LOCATION` gets the Router's own address. Then it makes one call, `POOLMANAGER.unlock(callbackData 5 order 0)`, and ignores the result. That call data is the encoded `SwapCallback` with action 5 (`PoolLiquidityFill`), the order and `maxMatches = 0`.
- **`fillFromPoolLiquidity_revert_iff`** (guards): the function has no checks of its own, so it reverts exactly when `unlock` reverts, with the same error.
- **`fillFromPoolLiquidity_ok_iff`** (footprint): on success, the end state is whatever `unlock` leaves, starting from the state after the two transient writes. The Router writes no persistent storage itself.
- **`fillFromPoolLiquidityPre_get`**: assuming `ext.get` reads back what `ext.set` wrote, those two writes change only the `transient` field.

These proofs cover the behaviour above; they don't establish that the function is safe overall. The function has no access check, so anyone can call it. Whether that is safe depends on how the `unlockCallback` side handles the `PoolLiquidityFill` action, which this item doesn't cover.
properties.title: Router.fillFromPoolLiquidity

properties.description:
**What is proved:**
- **Who can call it:** any caller other than `poolManager` gets `NotPoolManager`.
- **Pool must include the numeraire:** if neither currency is the numeraire, the call reverts with `NumeraireRequired`.
- **Pool must use a dynamic fee:** if `key.fee ≠ DYNAMIC_FEE_FLAG`, the call reverts with `DynamicFeeRequired`.
- **Exact success result** (`beforeInitialize_run_ok`): when all three checks pass, it returns `0xdc98354e` (the `beforeInitialize` selector). The resulting world is the three writes the generated code makes, in order. This theorem needs no extra assumptions.
- **Succeeds exactly when the three checks pass** (`beforeInitialize_succeeds_iff`). A companion theorem shows that any success returns the selector and leaves the stated storage.
- **What it changes** (`beforeInitialize_frame`): only the `poolManager`, `numeraire` and `feeVault` fields of `asyncOrders[key.toId()]` change. Every other pool and every other state variable is untouched.

The storage-level results assume only that reading the hook's storage back returns what was just written (`ext.get (ext.set w s) = s`). There are no external calls.

**Housekeeping:** I left two empty files, `formal/Scratch_BeforeInit.lean` and `formal/tmp_snippet.txt`. I couldn't delete them with the tools I have, so please remove them.

**Next:** the order create, fill and settle paths are where your self-fill concern actually matters. I'd prove there that no order can take out more than its maker put in.
properties.title: BaseHook.beforeInitialize

properties.description:
What the theorems show:
- **Reverts only on its two guards.** It reverts exactly when `msg.sender` isn't an executor that `order.owner` authorised on the order's pool, or when the stored order has `amountIn = 0`. A failing fill doesn't make it revert, because the `try/catch` swallows it.
- **Passes the checked order on unchanged.** When both guards pass, the result is exactly the self-call `this.fillOrderFromPoolLiquidity(order, id)`, made with the same `order` and the same `id` the guard just checked (the hash of chainid, pool id, owner, zeroForOne and salt).
- **Success returns `true`; a failed fill changes nothing.** If the fill succeeds it returns `true` with the fill's resulting state. If the fill reverts it returns `false` and the state is exactly as before the call.
- **Writes no storage of its own.** If the fill leaves this contract's storage unchanged, so does this function.

For your concern about someone filling their own order to drain other users' funds: this wrapper can't be used to fill a different order than the one it checked, and a caller who isn't an authorised executor can't fill anyone's order through it. A failed fill can't leave partial changes behind either. What I haven't proved yet is whether the fill itself, `fillOrderFromPoolLiquidity`, can pay out more than the order escrowed. That's still open, and it's the next item to take.

I also added a small helper lemma (`run_tryCatch`) that evaluates `try/catch` in the model. The other `tryCatch` site in the generated model can reuse it.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.tryFillOrderFromPoolLiquidity

properties.description:
What the theorems show:
- **Exact behaviour (`redeem_run`):**
  - It reverts with `ReentrantRedemption` if `_redeeming` is already set.
  - Otherwise it reverts with `InvalidRedemption` if the recipient or the amount is 0.
  - Otherwise it calls `poolManager.unlock(abiEncode [msg.sender, recipient, amount])` with `_redeeming = true`. A revert from that call comes back to the caller unchanged. On success the result is the call's final state with `_redeeming` cleared.
- **The two guards on their own:** `redeem_reentrant` and `redeem_invalid`.
- **When it succeeds (`redeem_ok`):** both guards passed, and the owner word sent to the pool manager is always `msg.sender`. No argument lets a caller name someone else as owner.
- **When it reverts (`redeem_reverts_iff`):** exactly when one of the guards fails or the pool-manager call reverts.
- **Storage written (`redeem_ok_state`):** this assumes a well-behaved storage accessor, i.e. reading back what was just written gives the same value. Under that, the external call sees `_redeeming = true`, and it is `false` again after a successful run.
- **Re-entry (`redeem_nested_reverts`):** any nested `redeem` made during the call reverts with `ReentrantRedemption`.
properties.title: NativeClaims.redeem

properties.description:
**Guards.** Each theorem names `AsyncSwap.setExecutorWithSig` fully qualified and covers one outcome:
- **Expired:** if the deadline has passed, it reverts with `SignatureExpired`.
- **Nonce used:** if `nonceUsed[maker][nonce]` is already set, it reverts with `NonceAlreadyUsed`.
- **Bad signature:** if the signature check rejects it for `maker`, it reverts with `InvalidSignature`.
- **Success:** otherwise the call burns the nonce and writes `asyncOrders[key.toId()].isExecutor[maker][executor] = allow`, and nothing more.

**Who can change what (`_ok_inv`, `_ok_state`, `_frame`, `_no_replay`):**
- **Needs the maker's signature:** a call only succeeds if the signature check returned true for `maker`. The signed message covers exactly the call's arguments: key, maker, executor, allow, nonce and deadline.
- **Writes only two things:**
  - It sets `nonceUsed[maker][nonce]`, which was false before the call.
  - It sets `maker`'s own executor flag in this one pool to `allow`.
- **Leaves everything else alone:** other makers' executor flags, every pool's orders, every other pool, the price books, `owner`, `pendingOwner` and every other nonce stay the same. So this function can't move funds or give anyone authority over another user's orders.
- **No replay:** once a call succeeds, any later call with the same `(maker, nonce)` reverts, whatever the other arguments or signature.

**Assumptions.** The last three properties rely on two things. First, `ext.get` returns what `ext.set` wrote. Second, three helpers the model leaves as black boxes don't change storage: the struct hash, `toTypedDataHash` and the ERC-1271 `staticcall`. In Solidity the first two are `pure` and the third is a `staticcall`, so this holds on chain, but the proof takes it as given. Inside the model I proved that the ECDSA recovery, `isValidSignatureNow` and `_hashTypedDataV4` don't change storage either, given those assumptions.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.setExecutorWithSig

properties.description: I proved plan item 16: `NativeClaims.unlockCallback` matches its slice. The proofs are in `formal/Refinement/Swarm/NativeClaimsUnlockCallback.lean`, and `lake build Refinement.Swarm.NativeClaimsUnlockCallback` passes with no `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide` or new axioms.
properties.title: NativeClaims.unlockCallback

properties.description:
- **Full run (`collect_run`):** the function first asks the hook for its owner, and if that read fails, the function fails the same way. Otherwise:
  - a caller who isn't the owner gets `Unauthorized`;
  - a zero recipient gets `ZeroAddress`;
  - otherwise it calls `poolManager.unlock(abi.encode(currency, recipient))` on the unchanged state, and the final state is whatever that call leaves.
- **Footprint:** FeeVault has no storage of its own, so the pool-manager call is its only effect.
- **Each guard on its own:** `collect_owner_view_reverts`, `collect_unauthorized` and `collect_zero_recipient`.
- **Success (`collect_ok`):** a successful call means the caller is the owner, the recipient is nonzero, and the pool manager got exactly `abi.encode(currency, recipient)`.
- **Revert conditions (`collect_reverts_iff`):** the function reverts exactly when one of those four steps fails.
- **Access control (`collect_only_owner`):** every successful call came from `hook.owner()`.
properties.title: FeeVault.collect

properties.description:
- **What a call does:** `unlockCallback_run` describes a call step by step:
  - It reverts `Unauthorized` unless the caller is the pool manager.
  - It reverts `abi.decode` unless `data` has at least 64 bytes and both words fit in an address.
  - It then reads the vault's own claim balance for that currency. If that read reverts, the callback reverts with the same reason.
  - If the balance is 0, it changes nothing and returns `""`.
  - Otherwise it runs `burn(address(this), currency, amount)` and then `take(currency, recipient, amount)`. Either revert passes straight through, and the vault writes no storage of its own.
- **Guard and revert theorems:** separate theorems cover the wrong caller, bad data, a failing balance read, the zero-balance case, the non-zero case, and an exact list of when it reverts.
- **On success (`unlockCallback_ok`):** the return value is `""`. The final world is either unchanged (balance was 0) or exactly the one `burn` then `take` leave, using the same `amount`.
- **Your concern (draining via a crafted order):** `unlockCallback_take_eq_own_balance` shows that the amount sent out is exactly the vault's own fee balance for that currency, read just before. That amount is first burned from the vault's own account, never from another user's claim. `unlockCallback_burn_fails` shows nothing is taken out if the burn fails. Only the pool manager can call this function.

The proofs assume nothing about how the pool manager's `burn`, `take` and `balanceOf` behave; they are left open. So these results say what the vault asks the pool manager to do, not how the pool manager carries it out.
properties.title: FeeVault.unlockCallback

properties.description: I proved plan item 19: `Router.swapWithSig` behaves exactly as its slice says. The proofs are in `formal/Refinement/Swarm/RouterSwapWithSig.lean`, and `lake build Refinement.Swarm.RouterSwapWithSig` passes with no `sorry`, `admit`, `native_decide` or new axioms.
properties.title: Router.swapWithSig

properties.description:
What the theorems show:
- **Guards, in order:**
  - An expired deadline reverts with `SignatureExpired`.
  - A used `(owner, nonce)` pair reverts with `NonceAlreadyUsed`.
  - If the `HOOK.asyncOrderInfo` view reverts, the whole call reverts.
  - A signature that doesn't check out for `order.owner` reverts with `InvalidSignature`.
- **Success:** the call ends in one `POOLMANAGER.unlock(SwapCallback(Cancel, order, 0))`.
- **Inversion (`cancelWithSig_ok_inv`):** any call that succeeds passed every guard. That includes a valid signature from `order.owner` over the digest binding the owner, both tokens, the hook's live `amountIn`, the order id, the nonce and the deadline.
- **Footprint (`cancelWithSig_ok_state`):** the only storage the Router writes before handing off to `unlock` is `cancelNonceUsed[order.owner][nonce] = true`. It writes no transient slot and moves no funds itself.
- **No replay:** using the same `(owner, nonce)` again reverts, whether re-entered from inside `unlock` (`cancelWithSig_reentry_reverts`) or called later (`cancelWithSig_no_replay`).

For your concern: anyone can submit a cancel for someone else's order, but it only goes through with the owner's signature, and each signature works once.

**Assumptions the theorems take as hypotheses:**
- The model leaves `toTypedDataHash` and the ERC-1271 signature check as opaque calls, so the footprint and no-replay results assume they don't change storage. Both are pure or static calls in Solidity.
- The after-the-call no-replay result also assumes `unlock` never sets a used cancel nonce back to `false`. The Router has no code that does.
properties.title: Router.cancelWithSig

properties.description:
What the theorems establish:
- **`cancelOrder_run`**: the function's complete behaviour. It reverts with `NotAuthorizedExecutor` unless the caller is the order's owner or an executor the owner approved in that pool. It reverts with `OrderNotFound` if the stored order amount (`amountIn`) is 0. Otherwise it runs a fixed sequence: remove the order from the book, clear the order's storage slot, burn the hook's claim, then pay out and settle the priority fee.
- **`cancelOrder_unauthorized` and `cancelOrder_notFound`**: each of those two reverts, stated on its own.
- **`cancelOrder_ok`** (your concern about filling or cancelling your own order to drain other users): on success, the burn (from the hook itself) and the payout to the order's owner use the same amount in the same currency. That amount is the one in storage when the call starts, not the `amountIn` field the caller passes in. The order id is a hash that includes the owner, direction and pool, so a caller can only reach an order stored under their own address, or under an owner who approved them as executor, in the pool and currency it was created with.
- **`cancelOrder_reentry_reverts`**: the order's slot is cleared before the first external call. So cancelling the same order again, including re-entering during the burn, always reverts and can't pay out twice.

Limits of these proofs:
- The book-removal step is a black box in the generated model. That is where the third guard (`PriceLevelMissing`) and the `orderCount`/`openOrderCount` decrements happen, so none of that is proved here.
- The external pool-manager calls are also black boxes. The theorems fix their arguments and order, not what they do.
- The re-entry result assumes that writing our storage and reading it back returns what was written.
- The same goes for the "owner-only" point: it assumes the hash used for the order id doesn't collide.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.cancelOrder

properties.description: Two parts of the model can't be seen into, so the proof doesn't cover them. The book-removal step (`_remove`), including its counter decrements and the `PriceLevelMissing` check, is treated as a black box. The model also doesn't say what the token manager's take-back and payout calls do inside, so I've only shown what they're called with. The re-entry proof also assumes that reading storage right after a write returns the written value.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.cancelOrder

properties.description:
**What the proofs show:**
- **Exact behaviour:** `updatePrice_run` says the function does exactly this: it reverts with `NotOrderOwner` unless the caller is the order's owner, then with `ZeroAmount` if the new minimum output is 0, then with `OrderNotFound` if the stored order has no input. Otherwise it removes the order from the book, updates it, and adds it back.
- **Each revert on its own:** `updatePrice_notOwner`, `updatePrice_zero` and `updatePrice_notFound`.
- **Success case:** `updatePrice_ok` shows a successful call came from `order.owner` with a non-zero new minimum on an order that has input. Between removing and re-adding, the only changes are to that order's minimum output, price and sequence number, plus the pool book's next sequence number. The new price is always between 1 and 2^128, and the sequence counter can't overflow (it's checked against uint64).
- **Nothing else changes:** the order's deposited input, owner, side and priority-fee fields stay the same, and so do every other order, every other pool, ownership, nonces and the book's open-order count and ordering mode.

**Your self-fill / sweep concern:** this function makes no external call and moves no tokens. It never changes the deposited `amountIn`. The order id is built from the owner's address, and only the owner may call it (not even an approved executor). So nobody can reprice someone else's order, and a reprice can't inflate what an order can later take out.

**Limits:**
- **Book code not covered:** removing and re-adding the order happen in code the model treats as a black box. That's where the two price-tree checks from the function's slice (`leafId == 0`, `id == 0`) and the order-count changes live, and none of it is proved here.
- **Storage assumption:** the success theorems assume that storage reads return what was last written.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.updatePrice

properties.description:
**The full behaviour, proved as one equation (`recordPriorityFee_run`).** The call reverts in exactly three cases:
1. No match is pending (the pending order id is 0), or the caller isn't the pending match's executor. Both values come from transient storage, not from the call's arguments.
2. The stored order's owner isn't the `maker` passed in.
3. The order has no input left, its fee is already escrowed, `amount` differs from the order's stored `priorityFee`, or `amount` is 0.

Otherwise it does three things, in order:
- mints exactly `amount` of the numeraire as claims to the protocol's own address;
- sets that one order's `priorityFeeEscrowed` flag to true;
- in priority-fee ordering mode only, removes the order from its price level and re-adds it.

**What this means for your self-fill concern:**
- **Who can call it:** only the pending executor, only for the pending order, and only if that order really belongs to the named `maker` (`recordPriorityFee_unauthorized`, `recordPriorityFee_wrong_maker`).
- **How much is credited:** exactly the order's stored fee, never a number the caller picks, and only to the protocol itself. No third party is paid and nothing leaves the protocol (`recordPriorityFee_amount_mismatch_reverts`).
- **No double counting:** the flag write changes only that one order's flag. Other orders, other pools, the price books and transient storage are untouched (`flagWorld_frame`). Once the flag is set, any further call for that order reverts, whoever calls and whatever arguments they pass (`recordPriorityFee_escrowed_reverts`, `recordPriorityFee_twice_reverts`).
- `recordPriorityFee_ok` gives all of the above as consequences of a successful call.

**Limits:**
- In the generated model, the remove/re-add step and the PoolManager mint are opaque, so their internal effects (price-tree updates, order counters) are not covered here.
- The frame and no-double-escrow results assume the model's storage accessor behaves normally (reading back a write returns what was written).
- Within the model, an order's fee can be credited to the protocol only once, and only for the stored fee amount.

Next: the plan's next item.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.recordPriorityFee
AsyncSwap.executeOrder

properties.description:
**Guards (when it reverts):**
- **`NotSelf`:** if the caller isn't the contract itself.
- **`OrderNotFound`:** if the stored order has `amountIn = 0`.
- **`NoActiveLiquidity`:** if the pool's liquidity reads 0. In that case no swap is attempted.
- **`PartialLiquidityFill` and `LimitPriceNotMet`:** these are proved from the success side. Any call that succeeds was a full fill at or above the limit (see below).

**On success**, the theorem gives the exact sequence of calls and what each is handed:
- The escrowed input claims are burned from this contract: exactly the stored `amountIn`, in the input currency.
- The pool's LP fee is set to 3000.
- There is one exact-input swap with `-amountIn` and price limit MIN+1 or MAX-1.
- The LP fee is put back to the value read from the pool before the swap.
- The swap used exactly `amountIn`, `amountIn < 2^127`, the output is positive and `out ≥` the stored `amountOutMin`.
- `out` of the output currency goes to the stored owner (`mint` if native, `take` otherwise), never a calldata field.
- Then the order is unlinked from the book (`_remove`), `orders[id]` is reset to default, and the escrowed priority fee is settled.

**Storage it writes (footprint):**
- The contract's own writes go only through the setters for `asyncOrders[pid]` and `priceBooks[pid]`, plus the direct reset of `orders[id]`.
- The order slot is cleared before the priority-fee settlement makes its external calls, so re-entering to fill the same order from there reverts.
- This needs the model's storage read-back law (`ext.get (ext.set w s) = s`) as a hypothesis.

**Limits:** the external calls and `_remove` are opaque in the generated model. So the guard on a missing price level (`PriceLevelMissing`) and the order-count decrements inside `_remove` aren't proved here. I also can't say anything about storage the PoolManager changes, including through re-entrant hook calls during the swap.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.fillOrderFromPoolLiquidity

properties.description:
**What is proved:**
- **Exact unfolding** (`updatePriceWithSig_run`): the function equals `_verify` over the signed message, then the `ZeroAmount` check, then the `OrderNotFound` check, then the existing `tail` from the `updatePrice` proof (remove, write, append). The signed message covers owner, tokens, the stored `amountIn` read before verification, the new minimum output, order id, nonce and deadline.
- **Each revert:** expired deadline (`SignatureExpired`), used nonce (`NonceAlreadyUsed`), rejected signature (`InvalidSignature`), zero new minimum (`ZeroAmount`), missing order (`OrderNotFound`). The not-the-owner check can never fire, because the function passes `order.owner` itself as the caller; the signature is the only authorization.
- **A missing order or a zero minimum always reverts**, whatever the signature.
- **Success** (`updatePriceWithSig_ok`): the deadline held, the nonce was fresh, and the signature check accepted the signature for `order.owner` over that exact message. Storage is then the nonce marked used, then remove, then the new minimum output, a price key in [1, 2^128) and a non-overflowing uint64 sequence, then append. The only external call is the ERC-1271 check, made with the owner, the digest and the signature.
- **No replay** (`updatePriceWithSig_burns_nonce`): after success, `nonceUsed` is the old map with exactly (owner, nonce) set, and any later call with the same owner and nonce reverts.

**What the proofs assume:**
- Writing storage and reading it back gives what was written.
- The typed-data hash and the ERC-1271 check change no storage. The hash is `pure` and the check is a `staticcall`, but the model leaves both abstract.
- For the no-replay theorem only: the remove and append steps, which the model also leaves abstract, don't change `nonceUsed`.
- The two tree guards in the slice (`leafId == 0`, `id == 0`) sit inside remove and append, so these proofs don't cover them.

The next open item is `BaseHook.beforeSwap`.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.updatePriceWithSig

properties.description:
The generated def only covers part of the function. `_createOrder` is left as an unexplained black box in the model, so 4 of the slice's 9 guards can't be proved here: `isExecutor`, the zero-amount check, the priority-fee rules and the node-id overflow. Those need a proof about `_createOrder` itself.

**What's proved:**
- **Reverts, in order:**
  - `NotPoolManager` unless the caller is the pool manager.
  - `ExactInputOnly` when `amountSpecified > 0`.
  - A `0x11` overflow panic on negating `type(int256).min`.
  - `abi.decode` when the hook data is shorter than 128 bytes or the user or executor word isn't a valid address.
  - An executor-mismatch revert when `sender` isn't `hookData.executor`. The model gives it an empty reason string rather than `NotAuthorizedExecutor`.
- **Success:** `beforeSwap_run_ok` shows that once those checks pass, the call is exactly `poolManager.mint(this, specified, amountTaken)`, then `_createOrder(poolId, zeroForOne, amountTaken, decoded hookData, specified == numeraire)`, then a return. `beforeSwap_ok_inv` and `beforeSwap_succeeds_iff` give the converse: it succeeds exactly when those checks hold and both calls succeed.
- **Return value:** always `(0x575e24b4, delta, 0)`. The escrowed amount is exactly `-amountSpecified`. When that amount is below 2^127, the delta is exactly `amountTaken × 2^128`.
- **Storage:** the function writes nothing itself. Every change to `asyncOrders` or `priceBooks` comes from the `mint` call or `_createOrder` (`beforeSwap_frame`).

The model also drops event emits, so it misses one revert: in Solidity, `toInt128` inside the `HookSwap` emit reverts when the amount is 2^127 or more. The real contract is stricter there, so that's not a bug, and the file's header says so.
properties.title: BaseHook.beforeSwap

properties.description:
What the theorems show:
- **It only hands off to the library** (`matchBook_eq`): the function is exactly `AsyncMatching.matchBook` working on `asyncOrders[key.toId()]` and `priceBooks[key.toId()]`, with `hook = address(this)`. Same return value, same final state.
- **Guard** (`matchBook_invalidBound`, `matchBook_bound_noOk`): `maxMatches = 0` or `maxMatches > MAX_MATCHES_PER_CALL` (which is 8) reverts with `InvalidMatchBound` before any storage is touched.
- **Return value** (`matchBook_ok`): on success, `1 ≤ maxMatches ≤ 8` and the returned match count is at most `maxMatches`. So the unchecked `uint8` counter `++matched` can never wrap. This comes from a loop invariant over the generated `for` loop.
- **Footprint** (`selfSet_frame`, `bookSet_frame`): the storage setters handed to the library write only that one pool's `asyncOrders` or `priceBooks` slot. Every other pool, field, `owner`, `pendingOwner`, `nonceUsed` and transient storage stays the same. This holds as long as the model's `get` returns what `set` just stored.

Limits:
- The other two guards in the slice (`leafId == 0` and the node-ID overflow) sit inside price-tree, `_remove` and `bestAtPrice` code that the model leaves opaque, so they aren't proved here.
- What the external calls (`donate`, `burn`, `settle`, `take`, `mint`) do is whatever the model's assumptions say; nothing is proved about them.
- `AsyncSwap.matchBook` has no caller check, unlike `fillOrderFromPoolLiquidity`. I didn't judge whether that is intended.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.matchBook
AsyncSwap.matchNewOrder

properties.description:
- **Full behaviour:** `getHookPermissions_run` shows that in any environment and storage state, the call succeeds, leaves storage unchanged and returns a fixed permission set. The proof is `rfl`, i.e. it holds by unfolding the definition.
- **No guards:** `getHookPermissions_never_reverts` shows it can never revert.
- **No writes:** `getHookPermissions_ok_iff` shows a successful result means exactly that fixed set and unchanged storage.
- **Returned flags:** `getHookPermissions_fields` checks every flag. Only `beforeInitialize`, `beforeAddLiquidity`, `beforeSwap` and `beforeSwapReturnDelta` are true; the other ten are false. This matches the Solidity at `src/AsyncSwap.sol:193`.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.getHookPermissions

properties.description:
The proof is in `formal/Refinement/Swarm/AsyncSwapAsyncOrder.lean`. Each theorem names `AsyncSwap.asyncOrder` in its statement:
- **`asyncOrder_run`:** for any environment and world, the function succeeds and returns `asyncOrders[poolId].orders[orderId].amountIn`. The world comes back unchanged.
- **`asyncOrder_never_reverts`:** it has no guards and never reverts.
- **`asyncOrder_ok_iff`:** it succeeds with result `a` and world `w'` exactly when `a` is that stored `amountIn` and `w'` is the starting world, so it writes nothing.
- **`asyncOrder_reads_only_asyncOrders`:** two worlds that agree on `asyncOrders` give the same result, whatever the environment. So `asyncOrders` is the only storage it reads.

It makes no external calls.
properties.title: AsyncSwap.asyncOrder

properties.description:
The function has no guards, which matches its slice. Every theorem names `AsyncSwap.asyncOrderInfo` fully qualified:
- **`asyncOrderInfo_run`:** in any environment and storage state, the call succeeds, leaves storage unchanged and returns `(amountIn, amountOutMin)` for `asyncOrders[poolId].orders[orderId]`. Lean accepts this by direct computation on the def (`rfl`).
- **`asyncOrderInfo_never_reverts`:** the call never reverts.
- **`asyncOrderInfo_ok_iff`:** it succeeds with exactly that pair, and the storage afterwards equals the storage before, so it writes nothing.
- **`asyncOrderInfo_reads_only_asyncOrders`:** the result depends only on `asyncOrders`. Two storage states that agree there give the same answer, whatever the environment.

properties.description:
The proof covers a side of the book `T`, which is `priceBooks[poolId].bids` when `isBuy` is true and `.asks` otherwise:
- **Full characterization (`bestOrder_run`):** `AsyncSwap.bestOrder` is described exactly.
  - If `T.root = 0`, it returns `(false, 0, 0, 0)` and changes no state.
  - Otherwise it walks down from the root, going right on bids and left on asks, to the first leaf `c`.
  - If no leaf turns up within the model's `loopBound` of 2^64 steps, it reverts with `"loop bound"`. That limit stands in for running out of gas, and it's the only revert in this function's own code.
  - Once a leaf is found, it returns `(true, p, orderId, maker)`, where `p` is the leaf's price, `orderId` is what `bestAtPrice(book, isBuy, p)` returns, and `maker` is the owner stored for that order.
- **Corollaries:** `bestOrder_empty` covers the empty side and `bestOrder_loopBound` the revert. `bestOrder_ok` gives the success shape: the leaf is reached from the root in fewer than 2^64 steps, every node before it is a branch, and the result is exactly the values above.
- **Footprint:** the tree walk (`best_run`, which works for any read-only accessor) never writes storage. `bestAtPrice` is treated as an opaque step in the generated model, so `bestOrder_readOnly` shows the whole call changes nothing only under the assumption that `bestAtPrice` is read-only. That matches Solidity, where it is a `view`, but the theorem relies on it rather than proving it.

properties.description:
AsyncSwap does not override `_afterInitialize`, so this function always reverts and never writes storage, returns a value or makes an external call. That is expected for a hook AsyncSwap doesn't implement, so I don't treat it as a bug. Each theorem names `BaseHook.afterInitialize`:
- **`afterInitialize_notPoolManager`:** if the caller isn't the pool manager, it reverts with `NotPoolManager`.
- **`afterInitialize_hookNotImplemented`:** if the caller is the pool manager, it reverts with `HookNotImplemented`.
- **`afterInitialize_spec`:** the exact result: it always reverts, and the caller decides which error.
- **`afterInitialize_never_ok`:** it never succeeds.

- **`beforeAddLiquidity_spec`:** combines the two: it reverts exactly when the caller is not the pool manager, and otherwise returns the selector.
- **`beforeAddLiquidity_frame`:** any successful call returns the selector, leaves storage untouched, and must have come from the pool manager.

- **`beforeRemoveLiquidity_hookNotImplemented`:** if the caller is the pool manager, it reverts with `HookNotImplemented`.

- **`beforeRemoveLiquidity_never_ok`:** there is no successful run, so it writes no storage, returns nothing and makes no external calls.

This function can never succeed. AsyncSwap doesn't override `_afterRemoveLiquidity`, so once the caller check passes, the default version always reverts. The four theorems all name `BaseHook.afterRemoveLiquidity`:

This isn't a bug. AsyncSwap's hook permissions set `afterRemoveLiquidity` to false (already proved in `AsyncSwapGetHookPermissions.lean`), so the pool manager never calls this function. I didn't need a PoC.

properties.description:
The proofs are in `formal/Refinement/Swarm/AsyncSwapCalculatePoolFee.lean`, and each theorem names `AsyncSwap.calculatePoolFee` in full:
- **`calculatePoolFee_run`:** gives the exact behaviour for any input. It fails with panic `0x11` (arithmetic overflow) only if the source expression's result would overflow. Otherwise it returns that result and leaves the stored state unchanged.
- **`calculatePoolFee_ok`:** for any `amount < 2^256` (every valid `uint256`), the function never reverts, writes nothing and returns exactly `amount * 3 / 997`. So splitting the calculation in two loses no precision compared with the plain formula.
- **`calculatePoolFee_le`:** the returned fee is never more than `amount`, and the state comes back unchanged.
